newsitem.title: USA: Dole joins Clinton in support of chemical treaty.
newsitem.headline: Dole joins Clinton in support of chemical treaty.

text.p: Republican Bob Dole on Wednesday stood shoulder-to-shoulder with President Bill Clinton and an old soldier gassed in the First World War in urging Senate approval of a treaty banning chemical weapons.

The unusual show of bipartisanship, which brought Dole to the White House for the third time since he lost last year's election to Democrat Clinton, reflected the exceptional push the president is making to overcome conservative opposition to the Chemical Weapons Convention.

The White House pep rally that united the chief rivals in 1996 also put Vice President Al Gore side-by-side with the Republican he profoundly hopes will not run for the presidency in 2000, retired Gen. Colin Powell.
If the meeting demonstrated that politics makes strange bedfellows, it also showed there are occasions where Republicans and Democrats will work together.

It was a complete turnaround for Dole. On the campaign trail last year he had raised a lengthy list of objections to the treaty and helped force the Clinton White House to ask that the Senate postpone consideration.

But he said he was satisfied with clarifications agreed to by the administration, and that if he were still in the Senate he would vote for the treaty. "Is it perfect? No. But I believe there are now adequate safeguards to protect American interests," Dole said.

Powell, a bright star in U.S. politics, took aim at conservative arguments that the treaty would give potential adversaries access to American know-how in defending against chemical attacks. "Why are member states or signatory states encouraged to share defensive technology? Because chemical weapons are horrible -- what they do to people," he said.

Sitting in a wheelchair and breathing with the assistance of an oxygen tank as the politicians pressed the Senate to add the United States to the list of nations that have ratified the treaty was George Clark, a 94-year-old veteran of the First and Second World Wars and the Korean War.
Clark, a Marine corporal at the time, was exposed to mustard gas in an attack at Soisson, France, in July 1918 that killed or wounded every other member of his outfit.
